vjmwcp:243: Constraints are addition: writing more rules, wrapping more tools, connecting more MCPs, and splitting into more roles may look stronger in the short term, but in the long term they can trap the model in outdated abstractions. Removable on-site context is subtraction: value is not in thickness, but in letting the agent get closer to real context faster, misunderstand fewer abstractions, and recover easily from failure. Vercel is the extreme case—removing most specialized tools and keeping only a filesystem agent that can execute bash, letting Claude read Cube DSL directly with grep, cat, and ls, raised the success rate from 80% to 100%, while time, steps, and tokens all decreased. This is not "fewer tools is better," but rather the old harness made too many choices for the model.
xon8q5:167: Architect Ruofei (JiaGouX) in this article "Revisiting Harness Engineering" pulls Harness Engineering from a "new concept" back to the engineering site: when large models start reading files, calling tools, modifying code, running tests, and working across turns, how should the work site outside the model be set up? Core argument: what really needs to be designed is not constraints, but a work site that is clear, auditable, verifiable, rollback-capable, and where old constraints can be removed at any time.
